records.why: Two science problems in the supporting phenomena. (1) Githeri taking longer at high altitude was presented as a result of hydrogen bonding; it is caused by lower air pressure lowering the boiling point of water (Nairobi, about 1,795 m, is about 81 kPa, boiling point about 94 °C, checked with the Antoine equation log10 P(mmHg) = 8.07131 - 1730.63/(233.426 + T): 81 kPa = 607.6 mmHg gives T = 93.9 °C). (2) See next record for iodine.
records.group_headline: Supporting phenomena corrected: altitude and boiling water, and the iodine / salt iodisation claim
records.old: • Water's Mysteriously High Boiling Point: Water boils at 100 °C — far higher than expected for such a small molecule — because of hydrogen bonding between H₂O molecules. This is why Lake Victoria retains warmth overnight and why githeri takes so long to boil at high-altitude Nairobi compared to Mombasa, linking hydrogen bonding to everyday Kenyan cooking experience.
records.new: • Water's Mysteriously High Boiling Point: Water boils at 100 °C — far higher than expected for such a small molecule — because of hydrogen bonding between H₂O molecules. The same strong attractions help explain why a large body of water such as Lake Victoria warms up and cools down slowly. (A separate idea for a good student question: at Nairobi's altitude, about 1,800 m, the air pressure is lower and water boils at about 94 °C, so githeri takes longer to cook than in Mombasa. That is an air-pressure effect, not a difference in hydrogen bonding.)
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Chapter 10 (Liquids and Solids), vapor pressure and boiling point; NIST Chemistry WebBook, water phase data

records.why: Table salt is iodised with iodate or iodide salts, not iodine crystals, so the old wording was misleading. Also, "never conduct electricity in any state" is too strong (molten iodine conducts slightly); the lessons only need "does not conduct as a solid", which matches what is observed.
records.old: • Iodine — Solid that Sublimes and Doesn't Conduct: Iodine crystals (used in Kenyan health programmes for salt iodisation) are a shiny solid at room temperature but sublime easily and never conduct electricity in any state — demonstrating how weak Van der Waals forces between simple molecular structures produce low melting points and the absence of free charge carriers.
records.new: • Iodine — Solid that Sublimes and Does Not Conduct: Iodine is a shiny dark solid at room temperature that sublimes easily to a purple vapour and does not conduct electricity as a solid — showing how weak Van der Waals forces between I₂ molecules give a low melting point and no free charge carriers. (Iodised salt contains small amounts of iodate or iodide salts, not iodine crystals; iodine itself is the antiseptic in tincture of iodine.)
records.reference: WHO/UNICEF/ICCIDD, Assessment of iodine deficiency disorders and monitoring their elimination (salt iodisation with potassium iodate/iodide)

records.why: Three problems fixed in this field. (1) Xenon's relative atomic mass is 131, not 108 (boiling point -108 °C is correct). (2) I₂ (254) is about twice as heavy as Xe (131), so they are not "of similar mass"; the useful point is that I₂ has about twice as many electrons (106 vs 54) and boils about 290 °C higher (184 - (-108) = 292). (3) Heating iodine in a sealed flask is unsafe because the vapour pressure builds up; a loosely stoppered flask in a water bath below 60 °C is the standard school method. Checked values: Xe 131.29 u, bp -108.1 °C; I2 253.8 u, bp 184.3 °C.
records.group_headline: Iodine and xenon comparison corrected (wrong mass, "similar mass" was untrue) and the sealed heated flask replaced by a loosely stoppered one
records.old: Teacher places a few iodine crystals in a sealed flask and gently warms it over a hot water bath. Learners observe purple vapour forming directly from the solid with minimal liquid phase. They record observations using a 3-column table: 'What I saw | What I expected | What puzzles me.' ACTIVITY B — Boiling Point Data Analysis (12 min): Learners work in groups of 4 to analyse an extended data set on ARES (or printed worksheet) comparing boiling points across: noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr), hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), and Group VI hydrides. Each group plots a graph of boiling point vs. molecular mass for noble gases and identifies the trend. They then locate iodine's boiling point (184 °C) and compare it to noble gases of similar mass (Xe, 108 a.m.u. boils at −108 °C vs I₂, 254 a.m.u. boils at 184 °C)
records.new: Teacher places a few iodine crystals in a dry conical flask, closed with a loose stopper (never airtight while heated), and gently warms it in a hot water bath below 60 °C in a well-ventilated room. Learners observe purple vapour forming directly from the solid with minimal liquid phase. They record observations using a 3-column table: 'What I saw | What I expected | What puzzles me.' ACTIVITY B — Boiling Point Data Analysis (12 min): Learners work in groups of 4 to analyse an extended data set on ARES (or printed worksheet) comparing boiling points across: noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr), hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), and Group VI hydrides. Each group plots a graph of boiling point vs. molecular mass for noble gases and identifies the trend. They then locate iodine's boiling point (184 °C) and compare it with xenon, the largest noble gas on the list (Xe: 131 a.m.u., 54 electrons, boils at −108 °C; I₂: 254 a.m.u., 106 electrons, boils at 184 °C)

records.old: (c) A copper wire could conduct because its sea of delocalised electrons carries charge, so copper would work as a conductor, although a metal is not the same as graphite as an electrode material. An NaCl solution conducts through mobile ions, but a liquid is not suitable as a solid electrode. Both are conductors, but the structure of graphite, a solid that conducts through delocalised electrons, is why it is chosen for the battery.
records.new: (c) Choice: NaCl solution. Verdict: it cannot replace graphite. A solution of NaCl does conduct, but only because its Na+ and Cl- ions are free to move, and ions cannot carry current through the wires of a circuit; the electrode must be a solid in which delocalised electrons carry the charge to the outside circuit. A liquid also cannot be shaped into a rod or hold its place inside a cell, and it would leak. Graphite does the job: its layers contain delocalised electrons, so it conducts as a solid, and its strong covalent bonding makes it chemically unreactive in the cell. (If copper is chosen instead: its sea of delocalised electrons means it conducts even better than graphite, so bonding supports it as a conductor, but copper is a reactive metal that can be attacked by the damp acidic paste in the cell, whereas graphite is unreactive, light and cheap, so graphite is the better electrode material.)
